title: {{NAME}} and the Stadium in the Wild
moral: The best stadiums aren't built of concrete, they're built of enthusiasm.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a vivid green-and-white soccer jersey, black shorts, and green cleats with white laces — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} was building a robot referee for the local junior league when his dog Moss dragged an injured fox into the garage.

The fox had a sprained leg, was unimpressed by the situation, and needed quiet rest.

{{NAME}} set it up in the corner.

His robot referee, REF, immediately started monitoring the fox's movements and temperature.

"That's not what you're for," said {{NAME}}.

REF beeped.

"Fair enough," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
The fox, recovering, watched practice sessions from the garage doorway with professional interest.

REF watched everything too, learning the patterns.

By week two, REF was making observations: "The fox's assessment of the ball trajectory is consistently more accurate than the players' adjustments."

{{NAME}} looked at the fox. The fox looked back.

"Are you analysing my football?" {{NAME}} asked.

The fox licked its nose.

"REF, can you translate that?"

"Insufficient data," said REF. "But its movement prediction accuracy is approximately ninety-two percent. For context: elite human players average sixty-three."

The fox watching from the garage doorway as {{NAME}} practices with a ball in the garden, REF tracking data on both of them with its sensors, {{NAME}} looking back and forth between them. pages.content:
He started including the fox in training.

Not playing exactly: the fox would position itself at the edge of the marked-out pitch and REF would relay its predicted optimal positions to {{NAME}}'s earpiece.

The fox was always right.

Moss, who had been watching, requested inclusion by sitting on the pitch in the goalkeeper position and refusing to move.

Moss turned out to be an exceptional goalkeeper: low centre of gravity, fast sideways movement, no concept of fear.

"This is the strangest training session I've ever run," said {{NAME}}. "REF, record everything."

pages.content:
By the end of the season, with REF calling tactical adjustments based on the fox's positional intelligence and Moss keeping goal with frightening competence, {{NAME}}'s team had the best defensive record in the league.

The league manager visited to ask about the team's unusual success.

"Good training methods," said {{NAME}}.

"Any specific methodology?"

{{NAME}} looked at the fox, who was sitting in its usual position. At Moss, who was guarding the garage. At REF, who was monitoring everything.

"Animal instinct and mechanical precision," he said. "And a dog who doesn't know the meaning of doubt."

pages.content:
At the end of the year, the fox's leg was fully healed.

{{NAME}} opened the garden gate one morning and the fox sat in the gap for a moment, looking back at him.

Then it was gone.

REF updated its tracking database: "Subject departed. Training record archived. Prediction accuracy: 91.7% over the season."

Moss sat by the gate and watched the space where the fox had been for a long time.

That evening, {{NAME}} lay in bed listening to the garden.

Somewhere, he was sure, a very clever fox was watching something move and knowing exactly where it would go.
